content: 1. The certainty of evidence regarding the effects of strict or intensive monitoring compared to routine monitoring with the Pinard fetal stethoscope is very low, as no included studies provide conclusive data. 2. Evidence from the Zimbabwe trial, which included 625 women and babies with risk factors for complications, was downgraded due to indirectness. 3. There is no evidence from the trial regarding maternal birth experience, including satisfaction, inability to adopt preferred positions during labor, or perceived loss of control during labor. 4. Evidence on perinatal hypoxia-ischemia, including Apgar scores less than 7 at 5 minutes, neonatal seizures, and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), is of very low certainty. 5. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that intensive Pinard monitoring probably reduces fetal distress, but the evidence is limited and of low certainty. 6. Long-term infant outcomes were not reported in the trial. 7. It remains uncertain whether increased identification of fetal heart rate abnormalities leads to improved birth and long-term infant outcomes. 8. Qualitative studies indicate that most women desire a normal childbirth with good outcomes for both mother and baby but acknowledge that medical intervention or assessment may sometimes be necessary. 9. Women prefer to receive relevant information from technically competent healthcare providers who are sensitive to their needs. 10. No research evidence on resource requirements for strict monitoring was found. 11. The Zimbabwe study suggests that more rigorous fetal monitoring may be more resource-intensive in terms of staff time. 12. WHO’s 2015 State of Inequality report highlights that women who are poor, less educated, and living in rural or remote areas have lower access to health interventions compared to more advantaged women. 13. In resource-limited settings, fetal heart rate monitoring is often less rigorous due to a lack of resources and poor quality of care. 14. Addressing fundamental quality of care issues with appropriate training, supervision, and monitoring could improve equity, regardless of the method of intermittent auscultation. 15. Women appreciate the intimate connection with healthcare professionals enabled by strict monitoring, provided it is conducted by kind, competent staff sensitive to their needs. 16. Healthcare professionals also prefer delivering woman-centered care if sufficient resources (staff) are available to support the labor-intensive nature of this approach. 17. Women would prefer competent staff to perform fetal monitoring in a way that detects fetal hypoxia in time to prevent poor outcomes. 18. Women may feel better cared for if their healthcare providers conduct strict monitoring of their baby’s well-being. 19. A qualitative systematic review found no feasibility concerns related to the intensive use of the Pinard fetal stethoscope. 20. Epidural analgesia is recommended for healthy pregnant women requesting pain relief during labor, depending on their preferences. 21. While evidence on the impact of epidural analgesia compared to no epidural analgesia for labor pain relief is limited, it is a proven method for relieving pain related to surgery, including abdominal surgery. 22. Women’s desire for epidural analgesia may be influenced by the clinical context, whether labor is spontaneous or induced, and their access to and knowledge of other pain relief options. 23. The care context, type of care provision, and care provider strongly influence the need for labor pain relief and the choices women make regarding this need. 24. Epidural analgesia is more effective for pain relief than opioid analgesia but requires more resources to implement and manage its adverse effects, which are more common with epidural analgesia. 25. To minimize complications and preserve motor function, the lowest effective concentration of local anesthetic should be used when administering epidural analgesia. 26. For women with epidural analgesia in the second stage of labor, facilitating a birth position of their choice, including an upright position, is recommended. 27. Delaying pushing for one to two hours after full dilation or until the woman regains the sensory urge to bear down is recommended for women with epidural analgesia in the second stage of labor. 28. Evidence on the effects of epidural analgesia on pain scores, pain intensity, or the need for additional analgesia during labor is very uncertain due to very low certainty of evidence. 29. It is unclear whether epidural analgesia affects instrumental births, as the certainty of this evidence is very low. 30. The impact of epidural analgesia on the duration of the first or second stages of labor compared to placebo is uncertain due to very low certainty of evidence. 31. It is uncertain whether epidural analgesia affects women’s perceived feelings of poor control during childbirth due to very low certainty of evidence. 32. Evidence on the relative effects of epidural analgesia compared to placebo or no intervention on side effects such as hypotension, vomiting, fever, drowsiness, or urinary retention is very uncertain. 33. It is uncertain whether epidural analgesia affects the number of babies born with Apgar scores of less than 7 at 5 minutes due to very low certainty of evidence. 34. Long-term outcomes, mother-baby interaction, and breastfeeding were not reported in the included studies. 35. Most women, especially first-time mothers, are apprehensive about childbirth and may welcome interventions that provide pain relief in certain contexts or situations. 36. Women want to be informed about the nature of interventions and, where possible, given a choice. 37. Women value epidural analgesia when it effectively alleviates labor pain and enables them to retain control over childbirth. 38. Some women fear receiving an epidural injection due to potential pain and complications, and there are mixed views on whether the pain relief provided is effective or ineffective. 39. Some women perceive that epidural analgesia helped them have a positive childbirth experience. 40. Women value the opportunity to make a choice about this method of pain relief and appreciate the support of professionals and family members for their decision. 41. All included qualitative studies on the use of epidural analgesia were conducted in high-income settings, with six studies undertaken in the USA. 42. It was not possible to identify whether women in the included studies had undergone augmentation, induction of labor, or other interventions that may have influenced their valuation of outcomes associated with epidural analgesia. 43. In some cultures, women may consider labor pain an integral part of childbirth and view physical expression of pain or discomfort as a sign of weakness. 44. Some women may view the use of epidural analgesia as an intervention that negatively impacts their sense of control during labor and childbirth. 45. No recent reviews on the costs and cost-effectiveness of epidural analgesia were found, but a 2002 USA review suggests that providing epidural analgesia for labor pain relief costs more than opioid analgesia. 46. The mean cost of a hospital-based vaginal birth in the USA was $3,117, with the incremental expected cost of providing epidural analgesia estimated at $338 (1998 values), primarily due to higher costs for healthcare professionals and increased costs associated with complications. 47. Findings from a Dutch study reported that birth costs were higher by €322 with routine epidural analgesia compared to analgesia on request, due to higher medication costs, longer hospital stays, and more cesarean sections and instrumental vaginal births. 48. The healthcare professionals required to administer and monitor epidural analgesia and perform instrumental births are likely the main cost component of this intervention. 49. Costs attributed to the procedure itself were much higher for epidural analgesia (€122) compared to opioid analgesia (€15).
